subject: ela
description: Students combine information that is presented in different media or formats (such as a chart, table, graph, timeline, map, diagram, photograph, or audio/video description) with information stated in the written text in order to build one coherent understanding of a topic or issue. They must read the words, read the non-text format, recognize how the two sources relate (confirm, extend, clarify, or contrast each other), and pull them together to answer a question that neither source fully answers alone.
subSkills: Read and interpret a non-text format described in the item (table, chart, graph, timeline, map, diagram, caption, photo description)
Identify the specific piece of information each format or source supplies
Recognize the relationship between the visual/quantitative source and the words (it confirms, adds to, clarifies, or contrasts the text)
Combine information from two or more sources to answer a question that requires both
Explain how a visual or quantitative element deepens or changes understanding of the written text
Distinguish information that comes only from the format from information that comes only from the words

problemArchetypes.name: Match the format to the text claim
problemArchetypes.example: A passage states that a city's population grew quickly after a new railroad opened. A described data table shows population figures by decade. The item asks which row of the table best supports the sentence in the text.

problemArchetypes.name: Fill the gap the words leave open
problemArchetypes.example: A passage describes how a glacier has been shrinking but never gives an amount. A described chart lists the glacier's length each year. The item asks the student to use the chart to state by how much the glacier shrank, then connect it to the text's claim.

problemArchetypes.name: Format clarifies a confusing or abstract statement
problemArchetypes.example: A passage explains that bees communicate direction by 'dancing' in patterns. A described diagram shows the angle of the dance relative to the sun. The item asks how the diagram helps the reader understand the sentence about direction.

problemArchetypes.name: Visual and words disagree or add a twist
problemArchetypes.example: A passage claims a sport is 'losing fans every year.' A described graph shows attendance actually rising in two of the last five years. The item asks how the graph complicates the claim made in the words.

problemArchetypes.name: Build a coherent answer from both sources
problemArchetypes.example: A passage describes the route early explorers took. A described map labels three landmarks. The item asks the student to use both the text and the map to put events in order or to identify where an event happened.

stimulusRules.selfContained: Every generated item must embed both the written passage AND a full description of the non-text format inside the item itself. Because the library is text-only, visuals are conveyed as clearly written descriptions or as small text tables/lists that the student reads in place. The student must need nothing external.
stimulusRules.formatRepresentation: Render tables as labeled rows and columns in text. Render graphs, charts, timelines, maps, and diagrams as a titled description that states every data point or labeled element the item depends on. Always title the format (for example 'Table 1: City population by decade') so the item can refer to it.

passageLength.easy: 3 to 5 sentences of text plus a small format with 3 to 4 data points or labels.
passageLength.medium: 6 to 9 sentences of text plus a format with 5 to 7 data points or labels.
passageLength.hard: 10 to 14 sentences (may be two short paragraphs) plus a denser or second format whose relationship to the text is not stated directly.

Easy.description: Short text and a simple format. The needed information is explicit in both sources and the relationship between them is direct: the format plainly confirms or restates a fact in the words. The student locates and matches; little inference is required.
constraints: Text is 3 to 5 sentences on a familiar, concrete topic
Format is one simple table, list, or single-trend chart with 3 to 4 entries
The visual directly confirms or supplies a fact the words point to
Answer is found by matching, not by reasoning across multiple data points

Medium.description: Longer text and a fuller format. The student must select the relevant data point from several and connect it to a specific claim, or use the format to fill a detail the words leave out. One step of inference is required to integrate the two sources.
constraints: Text is 6 to 9 sentences; topic may be less familiar
Format has 5 to 7 data points or labels, so the student must choose the relevant one
The format extends or clarifies the text rather than simply repeating it
Requires one inference to link the chosen data to the text's claim

Hard.description: Dense text plus a richer or second format whose relationship to the words is not stated. The student must evaluate how the sources interact, including cases where the format complicates, qualifies, or contrasts with the text, and build a coherent understanding from both. Multi-step inference and analysis are required.
constraints: Text is 10 to 14 sentences, possibly two short paragraphs, on an abstract or unfamiliar topic
Format is denser, or a second format is present, and its connection to the text is implicit
Task moves from identify to analyze or evaluate (how the visual changes, limits, or challenges the claim)
Requires combining two or more data points with the text to reach an answer neither source gives alone

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student uses only the written text and ignores the format entirely
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Answer is supported by the words alone and overlooks the data or label that the format adds, so it misses the integrated point.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student uses only the format and ignores what the words say
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Answer reports a number or label straight from the table or chart without connecting it to the claim in the text, treating the data as the whole answer.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student picks the wrong data point from the format
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Answer pulls a real but irrelevant figure from the format (a different row, year, or label) instead of the one that matches the text's claim.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student assumes the format must agree with the text and forces a match
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Answer claims the visual confirms the text even when the format actually contrasts with or complicates the claim.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student treats the format as decoration with no informational role
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Answer says the visual just makes the page look nicer or repeats the title, rather than identifying the specific understanding it adds.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student confuses which source supplied which fact
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Answer credits the words with information that came only from the format, or credits the format with a point made only in the text.
